title: The First Transcontinental Railroad
summary: Trace the ripples out from the 1869 golden spike: what caused the railroad, what happened right afterward, and what changed for years to come — for whom.
challenge: On May 10, 1869, two railroads met at Promontory Summit, Utah, and a golden spike joined the coasts by rail for the first time. A trip that once took months now took about a week. But every big change sends out ripples. What caused the railroad, what happened right afterward, and what changed later — and who was helped or hurt?

event.title: The Golden Spike — the railroad joins the coasts

causes: Congress passed the Pacific Railway Act (1862) to help pay for the tracks.
People wanted a fast, safe way to connect the East and West coasts.
Gold, land, and the chance to settle the West pulled people westward.
Trade and mail needed to move quickly across the whole country.
immediate: The golden spike joined the two railroads into one line.
Coast-to-coast travel dropped from months to about a week.
Goods, mail, and news moved much faster across the country.
New towns and stops grew up along the tracks.
longterm: Many more settlers moved west, and Western towns and farms grew.
Native nations lost land and hunting grounds, and the bison were nearly wiped out.
Chinese and Irish immigrant workers shaped the country but faced unfair treatment and low pay.
The railroad tied the nation into one big trade network and sped up its growth.
affected: The railroad companies — Central Pacific and Union Pacific
Immigrant laborers — Chinese (Central Pacific) and Irish (Union Pacific)
Native nations of the Plains and West
Settlers, farmers, and traders moving into the West

teacherText.keyideas: The Pacific Railway Act (1862) funded two companies — the Central Pacific (building east from Sacramento, largely with 10,000+ Chinese laborers) and the Union Pacific (building west from Omaha, largely with Irish, German, and Italian immigrants). They met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869. Travel fell from months to about a week. The benefits (faster trade, western settlement) came with heavy costs to Native nations and the bison, and hard, dangerous, underpaid work for immigrant laborers.
teacherText.misconceptions:
• The railroad was not built mainly by the men who got famous for it — immigrant laborers did most of the work.
• 'Opening the West' also meant taking land from Native nations who already lived there.
• The golden spike was ceremonial; it was removed right after the ceremony.
teacherText.vocabulary: transcontinental, Pacific Railway Act, Central Pacific, Union Pacific, Promontory Summit, immigrant labor, bison.
teacherText.context: Pacific Railway Act signed July 1, 1862; lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, May 10, 1869; locomotives Jupiter (CP) and No. 119 (UP); travel time coast-to-coast fell from ~4–6 months to about a week.
